sum: Teck Resources (TSX:TECK.B) is in focus after a packed late October update, which combined strong third quarter earnings, higher copper output and an affirmed dividend, despite recent labour and weather disruptions.

Recent trading reflects that mix of good news and fresh risks, with Teck Resources’ share price now at CA$85.38 after a 1-day share price return of 1.73% and a year to date share price gain of 29.38%. The 1-year total shareholder return of 49.21% signals stronger longer run momentum than the softer 90 day share price performance, which declined 7.95% as investors weighed strike action at Highland Valley Copper against the latest earnings and copper production update.

The recent pullback leaves Teck Resources trading at a double digit discount to both intrinsic value estimates and analyst targets. Is that a straightforward mispricing, or is the market correctly accounting for labour and weather risk?

Teck Resources last closed at CA$85.38 against a widely followed fair value estimate of about CA$95.38. This frames the current pullback as a discount that depends on how well its copper projects and merger plan are executed.

The Highland Valley Copper Mine Life Extension project is now largely engineered, with most procurement awarded and significant 2026 capital allocated. This supports a long production profile that can underpin revenue visibility and earnings from copper for Teck Resources.

items.t: How UK shares reacted to US midterm election result
London midday: FTSE surges as banks and miners rally
sum: London stocks had surged by midday on Wednesday, with banks and miners pacing the advance as investors mulled the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections.
The FTSE 100 was up 1.2% at 10,767.79. At the same time, sterling hit a seven-week high against the dollar, which fell against a number of currencies after the so-called blue tsunami.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said: "Investors are trying to get their heads around what a Democrat landslide in the US mid-term elections means for financial markets, with an initial stock sell-off quickly turning into gains.
"Theoretically, a divided government can create gridlock for policy changes, but there is a school of thought that Democrats may prioritise pushing through AI regulation.

"Given that AI has been the key to considerable stock market wealth creation in recent years, the prospect of red tape could put the brakes on this hot investment theme. However, a positive market reaction implies that certain investors are welcoming the potential that Trump’s political power may be curbed somewhat.

"The big risk is uncertainty around how Trump could act in the coming months following such a result. Gold jumped 2.7% to $4,038 per ounce, which suggests that investors have added a little protection to their portfolio as a ‘just in case’ precaution. The precious metal may also be responding to incipient fears that the Democrats may go on a spending spree if they get the chance.

"Brent crude nudged 0.3% higher to $103.88 per barrel, perhaps reflecting how Trump may now focus more on foreign policy, where he could have more sway than over domestic matters, and ratchet up tensions with Iran as a result. Higher commodity prices also gave a boost to the FTSE 100 where oil producers and miners led the charge alongside banks."

South Africa’s $30 billion succession: what the Rupert, Oppenheimer and le Roux heirs inherit
sum: The three men behind South Africa’s largest private fortunes are 76, 77 and 81. Their sons stand to inherit very different things, and only one of them is being groomed in public.

South Africa’s three largest fortunes belong to men born before 1951. Johann Rupert, chairman of Swiss luxury group Richemont, is 76 and worth roughly $15 billion on recent market estimates. Nicky Oppenheimer, 81, whose family controlled De Beers for more than 80 years, holds about $10.8 billion. Michiel le Roux, 77, co-founder of Capitec, has about $3.8 billion. Together they account for close to $30 billion, a sum that moves with the share prices of a Geneva-based luxury group and a Stellenbosch bank.

Each man has a son in line. The resemblance ends there. Anton Rupert, 39, is being placed inside the governance of a listed company his family controls with a minority of its equity. Jonathan Oppenheimer, 56, already runs a family office whose wealth was converted to cash 14 years ago. The younger Michiel le Roux built his own lender elsewhere in Africa and has no role at Capitec. For investors in Richemont, Remgro and Capitec, those differences decide how much a change of generation will be felt in the boardroom and on the share register.

On September 9, Richemont named Anton Rupert non-executive co-deputy chairman, with immediate effect. He shares the title with Bram Schot, 65, the former Audi chief executive who joined the board in 2023 and became deputy chairman in 2024. The board split the job. Schot handles governance and the coordination of board committees; Rupert oversees the Strategic Product and Communications Committee, which sets product and messaging priorities across Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and the group’s other maisons. Johann Rupert called the appointment “an important step in the Board’s long-term succession planning.”

The younger Rupert has sat on Richemont’s board since 2017 and has also served as a director of Remgro. He keeps a low public profile. His best-known roles have been at family concerns such as L’Ormarins, the Rupert wine estate in Franschhoek, and the Franschhoek Motor Museum.

items.t: Major European markets close mixed as investors react to earnings
sum: The major European markets closed mixed on Friday even as most of the other markets across the continent ended notably lower, as investors reacted to a slew of corporate earnings announcements and the latest batch of regional economic data.

Higher oil prices and weakness in the tech sector due to renewed uncertainty about returns on AI-related investments hurt sentiment. Disappointing earnings updates from Amazon and Intel weighed as well.
Brent Crude front-month futures rose above $114 a barrel, gaining about 3%, raising concerns about inflation and economic slowdown.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 ended down 0.36%. Germany's DAX settled lower by 0.85%. France's CAC 40 ended flat, while the UK's FTSE 100 edged up 0.07%. Switzerland's SMI finished with a gain of 0.36%.
Among other markets in Europe, Austria, the Czech Republic, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Turkey ended sharp to moderately lower.
Greece edged down marginally. Denmark, Norway and Russia closed on firm note, while Belgium ended flat.

In the UK market, NatWest Group tumbled nearly 9% after profit attributable to ordinary shareholders dropped 4.1% to 1.532 billion pounds from 1.598 billion pounds a year ago. Earnings per share were 19.1 pence, down from 19.6 pence last year.

The White House Should Question Beijing Cutting a Copper Deal in Our Backyard
sum: China is demanding copper guarantees in exchange for approving a mining megadeal. If the Donroe Doctrine still matters, the Trump administration should seek the same.

One of the biggest mining mergers in history faces one final hurdle before becoming a new metals titan: it must guarantee the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) a steady flow of copper for decades to come.
The question China hawks are asking is whether the Trump administration will let it slide or level the playing field by securing something in return.

Energy demand is climbing fast, and metals such as copper, nickel, and cobalt are growing in importance. Copper, above all, runs through our power grids, weapons systems, and data centers. Whoever controls that supply wields notable geopolitical power.

Today, China plays an outsized role in refining copper. It operates around 65 copper smelters, whereas Europe has 15 and North America just three. So, when two of the most powerful copper miners in the Western Hemisphere announced they’d be combining forces in September 2025, it should have caught Washington’s attention.

The deal in question is the $54 billion combination of London-based Anglo American and Canada’s Teck Resources. It has been cleared by every country where the companies operate except one—China. And now, China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has asked Anglo to commit a steady stream of copper concentrate to Chinese smelters as a condition for the merger’s approval.

While Anglo and Teck would control a large percentage of the global copper supply, China’s assurance request is not about protecting competition. It’s about leverage. Using the merger as a bargaining chip is a tactic to secure raw materials as the country experiences a historic shortage of feedstock.

items.t: Anglo American maintains copper guidance: what it means for Anglo American stock
sum: Anglo American (GB00BTK05J60) was trading at EUR 46.51 at Lang & Schwarz at 9:31 a.m. CEST on October 21, 2026. The mining group published its third-quarter production report on October 20, 2026, showing lower copper output but unchanged annual guidance, according to Anglo American.

Copper production fell 5.00 percent to 174,900 tonnes in the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, from 183,500 tonnes a year earlier. Record snowfall and related maintenance in Chile, together with lower-grade stockpile processing at Collahuasi, weighed on the quarter.

For the first nine months of 2026, copper production was 519,000 tonnes, down 1.00 percent from 526,000 tonnes in the comparable period. The company kept its 2026 copper production guidance at 700,000-760,000 tonnes, while Copper Peru unit-cost guidance fell to 50 US cents per pound from 65 US cents.

Management is still presenting the weaker quarter as compatible with its broader restructuring plan. Reuters reported on October 20, 2026, that the planned merger with Teck Resources remained subject to final approval in China, with completion timing unchanged at March 2027. Anglo American also said its Australian steelmaking coal sale to Dhilmar could deliver up to USD 3.875 billion and should complete by the first quarter of 2027.

On October 14, 2026, Anglo American reported that its dividend reinvestment plan involved 64,346 shares, according to Investegate. On October 20, copper production was reported at 174,900 tonnes, while the Teck transaction retained its March 2027 completion timing.

The next two dated milestones are the planned completion of the Australian steelmaking coal sale in the first quarter of 2027 and the expected Anglo-Teck merger completion by March 2027. Both dates remain conditional on transaction progress and regulatory steps.

Anglo American has a market capitalization of GBP 41.7 billion as of October 21, 2026. Its primary listing is in London, where the share price was GBp 3,895 at 7:33 a.m. UTC on October 21, 2026, according to the structured market quote.

Duncan Wanblad — CEO, Anglo American Corporation
sum: DUNCAN Wanblad’s 2022 appointment as Anglo American’s CEO was seen as a return to the company’s South African roots, but Wanblad had other plans. While defending against BHP’s bid for Anglo in 2024, Wanblad accelerated the company’s restructuring plans, which among other things saw the demerger of Anglo American Platinum. Fixated on copper – the commodity of choice for many these days – he capped 2025 off with a bold ‘merger of equals’ with Canada’s Teck Resources, which will be headquartered in Canuck land. Shareholder and Canadian regulatory approval clinched the $50bn takeover of Teck in December.

The new company Anglo Teck will have more than 70% exposure to copper, which is firmly in line with Wanblad’s strategic vision. In addition to seeing through the formation of Anglo Teck, Wanblad must also oversee the disposal of storied diamond giant De Beers, which has lost much of its shine in the face of surging demand for far cheaper lab-grown gems. The suitors include world No. 1 diamond producer Botswana, which has been pointedly warned by the International Monetary Fund not to raise its stake in De Beers. This is a tricky political egg as Angola and Namibia have expressed an interest in owning shares.

There’s also the question of Anglo’s metallurgical coal mines in Australia which remain unsold after Peabody Energy pulled its offer last year. Make no mistake, however, in just three years, Wanblad has completely altered Anglo and proved wrong the sceptics who thought he would remain in the shadow of his former boss, Mark Cutifani.

Wanblad is a supporter of English football club Watford but he may now find himself in the stands for the Vancouver Canucks ice hockey team. A keen cyclist, he will also find the Canadian Rockies a bracing challenge. Wanblad worked his way up through the Anglo ranks after joining associate JCI in 1990. Previous stints included a brief period as joint interim CEO at Anglo American Platinum in 2007. He became group director for strategy and business development and was finally appointed CEO in 2022.

Mountain Province Diamonds announces exit from N.W.T.'s Gahcho Kué mine
sum: Toronto-based Mountain Province Diamonds announced Thursday that it is giving up its 49 per cent ownership share of the N.W.T.'s Gahcho Kué diamond mine, handing full control over to De Beers Canada.

A news release from Mountain Province says that the restructuring agreement will release the company from all its financial obligations and liabilities related to the mine, while retaining the option to regain an ownership stake in the future.

"This agreement follows an extensive review of the alternatives available to the company against the backdrop of a material decline in diamond prices over the past year, driven in the main by tariff-related uncertainty and the conflict in the Middle East,” Jonathan Comerford, president and CEO of Mountain Province, said in a statement.

“It provides the most credible path to protect stakeholder value in the current circumstances,” Comerford stated, saying further that the company could return to the mine if market conditions improve.

Opened in 2016 as a joint venture between Mountain Province and majority owner De Beers, Gahcho Kué is the last active diamond mine in the Northwest Territories following the closures earlier this year of Rio Tinto’s Diavik mine and the Ekati mine, which is now in receivership.

Amid a global slump in the diamond market and the dwindling of the industry in the N.W.T., there have been indications of troubles for Mountain Province and Gahcho Kué, which is on a timeline for a planned closure by 2028.

Mountain Province voluntarily delisted its stocks from Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) in the summer and the mine saw a delay in a planned expansion earlier this year which lead to talks about the layoff of up to 5 per cent of the workforce.

Copper Stocks Tumble as Tariff Doubt Reverses Record Rally: Freeport-McMoRan Sinks 8%, Teck Resources and Southern Copper Drop 7%
sum: A single policy update with no operational content just sent the entire copper mining sector into freefall, erasing billions in gains that took months to build. Here is why tariff uncertainty can reprice a whole industry inside minutes.

Shares of Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE:FCX | FCX Price Prediction) are sliding early Thursday as a record rally in copper reverses inside a single session. Freeport-McMoRan stock is down 8% to $70.43 after reports cast doubt on the refined-copper tariffs that had powered the metal to fresh highs earlier this week. The scarcity trade that built up all summer is unwinding in real time, and copper miners are traveling with it.

The selloff runs deep across the group. Also under pressure, Southern Copper (NYSE:SCCO) stock is down 7% to $195.66, and Teck Resources (NYSE:TECK) stock is down 7% to $65.08. Both names had ridden the same setup that lifted the group into Tuesday’s records, and both are now handing back a meaningful piece of that move.

The Global X Copper Miners ETF (NYSEARCA:COPX) is down 7% as the entire basket rerates in unison, with its three largest U.S.-listed constituents leading the decline. Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.41%, so today’s damage is concentrated in copper names rather than the wider market.

Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange is down 3.1% to $14,312 per metric ton after touching a record $14,875 earlier in the same session. The reversal followed reports that the White House hasn’t yet reached a decision on tariffs covering refined copper, with officials weighing how higher prices would feed through into manufacturing costs. Precious metals are lower too, with a firmer dollar and higher inflation-adjusted Treasury yields weighing on the broader metals complex.

Expectations of tariff action had been a central plank of the rally, pulling U.S.-bound metal out of global warehouses and building a scarcity premium into the physical price. Remove that expectation, and the premium unwinds inside minutes, which is why a policy update with no operational content just repriced the entire mining group.

Copper price pauses below record as China's imports slump, mine supply heads for first drop since 2017
sum: Copper paused just below record territory on Wednesday after four straight sessions of gains carried the metal to all-time highs in New York and London, with the escalating conflict in the Middle East pushing Brent crude back above $100 a barrel and reviving worries about inflation ahead of Friday’s US consumer price data.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract, was up 0.5% at $6.8545 a pound (about $15,110 a tonne) by late morning in New York, after touching $6.8730 on Tuesday, the highest ever for a Comex contract and above the $6.7775 peak the September contract set on August 26. Tuesday’s settlement of $6.8235 was also a record.

In London, three-month copper slipped 0.4% to $14,645.50 a tonne by late morning after climbing to an all-time high of $14,779 on Tuesday and closing at $14,708, the second record in as many days after Monday’s push past the January peak of $14,527.50. The LME’s index of six base metals also set a record on Tuesday as zinc breached $4,000 a tonne for the first time since 2022. Aluminium, nickel and lead all eased on Wednesday.

China imported 382,000 tonnes of unwrought copper and copper products in August, down from 425,000 tonnes in July and the weakest August in six years, customs data show, taking the January to August total to 3.3 million tonnes, 6.7% below last year. The metal is going west instead. US imports of refined copper hit a record 225,094 tonnes in July, with Chile supplying 46% and a record 53,290 tonnes arriving from the Democratic Republic of Congo, even though no Congolese brand is deliverable against the Comex contract.

Traders have spent the year moving copper into the US ahead of a 15% duty on refined imports proposed for January 2027, rising to 30% in 2028, which Washington has neither confirmed nor ruled out more than two months after the Commerce Department was due to report. Comex warehouses held a record 695,624 tonnes on Friday, more than double the roughly 300,000 tonnes left in LME and Shanghai sheds combined. Shanghai’s 63,000 tonnes is the lowest since January 2024, and LME stocks have shed nearly 40% since late May.

Qualcomm Shares Jump on Multi-Generation AWS AI Chip Deal
sum: Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM), the chipmaker best known for smartphone processors, jumped in trading on Tuesday after it signed a multi-generation deal with Amazon’s AWS cloud unit to build custom AI chips and data-centre connectivity.
QCOM was up 4.5% at $176.33 during Tuesday’s session, from Monday’s close of $168.74, having traded as high as $183.49 and as low as $173.15 intraday.

Qualcomm and AWS, Amazon’s cloud computing division, announced a multi-generation collaboration to build customised silicon for large-scale AI inference and to co-develop optical connectivity for AWS data centres, extending up to 1.6 terabits per second. Bloomberg reported that as part of the deal, Qualcomm issued AWS a warrant to buy up to 25 million QCOM shares, worth as much as $4bn, at an exercise price of $161.26, vesting in tranches tied to as much as $60bn of cumulative chip orders from Amazon. Qualcomm chief executive Cristiano Amon said the company was “pleased to work with AWS on customized silicon and connectivity solutions, bringing decades of leadership in advanced processing and power-efficient compute, to deliver breakthrough performance and enable the next generation of AI infrastructure.”

The deal matters because Qualcomm is pushing to diversify away from handsets, where Apple’s share of the upcoming iPhone launch is now expected to come in well below the roughly 20% previously estimated, with Apple-related product revenue expected down around 50% quarter-on-quarter and QCT Android handset revenue down 20% year-over-year. Non-handset revenue growth is accelerating, from 24% in fiscal 2026 to more than 60% in fiscal 2027, and management is targeting $40bn in non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, with data-centre revenue guided to rise from $5bn in fiscal 2027 to $15bn by fiscal 2029. The warrant structure ties Amazon’s equity upside to Qualcomm actually delivering large chip orders, rather than handing over free shares, aligning the two companies’ incentives around execution.

Broadcom shares also rose alongside Qualcomm’s move, which market commentary read as validation of the wider custom AI silicon category rather than business shifting away from incumbent hyperscaler chip suppliers. Amazon’s own shares were little changed on the news.

sum: Shares in Molten Ventures PLC (LSE:GROW) climbed almost 2% to 695p on Monday, adding 12p, after the venture capital firm announced the first close of its new Growth Fund at £175 million.
The rally came as Molten confirmed the British Business Bank had committed £75 million as a cornerstone investor in the new fund.
Molten Ventures, which invests in high-growth technology companies across Europe and the UK, said it had committed the remaining £100 million of the first close.
The London-listed firm is targeting a final fund size of £350 million, with additional third-party investors still being sought.
Ben Wilkinson, chief executive of Molten Ventures, said the British Business Bank's backing was "a strong endorsement" of the company's strategy.
The Growth Fund will focus on Series B and later-stage investment rounds, targeting sectors including space, artificial intelligence, fintech, quantum computing, hardware and deep technology.

sum: Anglo American plc (GB00B1XZS820) stock is trading cautiously higher on August 19, 2026 as London-listed miners respond to the latest UK inflation reading and broader FTSE 100 moves. Recent market data shows the shares gaining 0.7% alongside other major mining groups as investors reassess cyclical exposure to metals and minerals in a shifting macro backdrop.

A fresh snapshot of UK consumer prices published for July 2026 has kept the FTSE 100 index in a cautious trading pattern on August 19, 2026, with heavyweight mining names contributing modestly to the move. Per a recent market overview covering that session, Anglo American and a peer added 0.7% each while another diversified miner advanced 0.5%, suggesting investors are selectively rotating into resource stocks despite a mixed index-level reaction to the inflation print. The incremental gain underscores how the group can benefit when inflation data reinforce expectations for resilient commodity demand.

While the FTSE 100 as a whole slipped 0.1% at 09:26 GMT on August 19, 2026, the positive contribution from mining stocks highlighted the sector’s potential as a partial hedge against price pressures. For Anglo American, the modest move may reflect a balance between concerns about cost inflation in operations and optimism that higher nominal pricing for key commodities such as iron ore, copper and platinum-group metals can sustain cash generation. In this environment, even a 0.7% single-session gain matters as investors compare cyclical names and track year-to-date returns in the mining segment.

To gauge Anglo American’s valuation backdrop, investors can look at both primary London trading and secondary references on global platforms. A recent analyst and recommendation overview tied to real-time CBOE data on August 19, 2026 cited a level of 3,868.50 GBX for the shares, with the five-day change at +0.93%, the year-to-date performance at +28.64% and the year-to-date change versus the start of 2026 also clearly positive. Those figures indicate that, even after periods of volatility, Anglo American has delivered a double-digit gain since January 2026, outpacing many broader equity indices and reflecting strong cyclical positioning.

Anglo American shares jump as copper cost guidance cut sharply
sum: Shares in Anglo American PLC (LSE:AAL) rose 5% to 3,703p after the FTSE 100 miner slashed its cost forecasts for its copper business, the division that will define the group after its merger with Canada's Teck Resources.
Unit cost guidance for copper, the cash cost of producing a pound of metal, was cut to about 145 cents from roughly 172 cents previously.
That reflects a reduction in Chilean costs to about 210 cents a pound from 230 cents, and a much steeper cut in Peru to about 65 cents from 100 cents.
The savings come from higher credits for by-products such as molybdenum, which are sold alongside copper and offset production costs, and from favourable currency movements.
Cost discipline matters more than volumes here, because Anglo is repositioning itself as a copper pure play and investors are focused on the margin the enlarged group can generate.
Realised copper prices in the first half were 608 cents a pound, 39% higher than a year earlier and above the average London Metal Exchange price of 593 cents.
Production itself was unremarkable, with copper output flat at 173,200 tonnes as higher throughput at Los Bronces offset lower ore grades at Collahuasi and Quellaveco.

Goldman Sachs Turns Positive on Glencore, Citing Copper and Zinc Strength (GLEN)
sum: Glencore PLC (LSE:GLEN) received an upgrade from Goldman Sachs on Thursday, with the investment bank raising its recommendation to Buy from Neutral. The broker said the diversified miner is well placed to benefit from favourable market conditions in copper, zinc and metallurgical coal, even as it remains cautious on the outlook for iron ore.
Shares in Glencore climbed 3.5% to 507.80 pence in London trading, comfortably outperforming the FTSE 100, which gained around 0.7% during the session.

Although Goldman Sachs reduced its 12-month price target to £6.30 from £6.60, it said the recent weakness across the mining sector has created a more attractive valuation. The revised target continues to indicate significant upside from the current share price.

According to the broker, Glencore offers one of the strongest combinations of exposure to its preferred commodities, together with potential earnings upside from its marketing division and an attractive valuation compared with other diversified mining companies.

Goldman expects copper prices to remain well supported by tightening global mine supply and the possibility of U.S. import tariffs. It also believes zinc fundamentals remain favourable due to ongoing shortages of concentrate supply. In addition, the bank has become more optimistic about metallurgical coal following supply disruptions in China's Shanxi province and expectations of seasonal restocking demand from India and China later this year.

The broker also highlighted additional upside potential from Glencore's marketing business, pointing to elevated volatility in energy markets and ongoing dislocations across the physical copper and aluminium markets. Goldman added that potential asset sales—including infrastructure holdings, Glencore's remaining stake in Bunge and selected mining investments—could provide additional capital for enhanced shareholder returns over the next 12 to 18 months.
Looking more broadly across the sector, Goldman Sachs reiterated its positive view on European mining companies with significant exposure to copper and aluminium.

items.t: FTSE 100 Live: Stocks plunge as oil spikes on Trump saying Iran ceasefire 'over'
Oil Price Spike July 2026: What It Means for UK Investors
sum: On 7 July 2026, drone strikes hit shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important routes for oil and gas, and prices jumped as a result, with Brent crude touching around $74 a barrel. Energy giant Shell also issued an upbeat trading update, sending its share price up over 3%, while mining stocks fell as investors got nervous about the wider picture.
If none of that means much to you yet, don’t worry! That’s exactly what this post is for.
We’ll explain what’s actually going on, why it matters even if you don’t own a single oil stock, and what beginner investors should (and shouldn’t) do about it.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water between Iran and Oman that a huge chunk of the world’s oil and gas passes through on tankers every day.

When there’s any hint of disruption there- like this week’s drone strikes on vessels- oil traders get nervous that supply could be cut off, so the price of oil rises even before any actual shortage happens. This is sometimes called a “geopolitical risk premium”: prices moving on fear of what might happen, not just on what has happened.

At the same time, Shell (one of the UK’s biggest companies and a major part of the FTSE 100) said its own trading was looking stronger than expected for the second quarter, partly because this kind of volatility can actually boost profits for energy traders. Its shares rose over 3% on the update. Mining stocks like Anglo American and Rio Tinto fell, reflecting broader nervousness about global growth and demand.
Even if you don’t own any energy shares, this story affects you in a few ways:

London close: Stocks finish higher but pare early gains as oil prices jump
sum: London's blue chip index inched higher on Tuesday, though gains were only minor as investors weighed a jump in the price of oil on the back of renewed attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

The FTSE 100 finished just 0.1% higher at 10,665.88, paring earlier gains which sent it to a high of 10,747.01 (+0.9%). The index slipped 0.3% on Monday after closing at 10,679.03 on Friday, its highest since early March.

Brent crude was up 2.6% at $73.86 a barrel by the close of play in London after a report that an LNG ship from Qatar was hit as it travelled through the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, another commercial vessel was hit by a projectile near the Omani coast as it exited the Strait, the UK's Maritime Trade Operations agency said.

"Renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz reignited concerns over global energy supplies and cast doubt on the durability of the US-Iran agreement," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG.
Market participants were mulling the latest results from Samsung, whose shares tumbled despite the South Korean chipmaker seeing second-quarter profits surge 1800%.

In a brief pre-earnings update, Samsung said that operating profits in the three months to June-end were estimated to have soared to 89.4trn won (£43.7bn), ahead of estimates and up from 4.7trn won a year previously, while revenues rocketed 129% at 171trn won..

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said: "Although Samsung’s results were stellar, investors are getting nervous about the scale of money ploughing into AI and whether it’s a bubble waiting to burst."
